args:
Research how to implement a fast BATCHED square Householder QR factorization as CUSTOM GPU kernels (Triton first, CUTLASS CuTe DSL for more control) on an NVIDIA B200 (compute capability 10.0, sm_100, CUDA 12.8, PyTorch 2.11). Do NOT recommend library calls (cuSOLVER/cuBLAS/MAGMA/CUTLASS prebuilt) as the answer — the goal is hand-written kernels; libraries are only useful as performance reference points and for understanding the blocked algorithm.

EXACT PROBLEM CONTRACT: Input A is a batch×n×n float32 CUDA tensor. Output must be (H, tau) matching torch.geqrf EXACTLY: H is batch×n×n FP32 with R in the upper triangle and the Householder reflector vectors below the diagonal; tau is batch×n FP32 reflector coefficients. A checker reconstructs Q = torch.linalg.householder_product(H, tau), takes R = triu(H), and validates (1) factor residual ‖R − Qᵀ@A‖ with rtol = 20·n·eps32 and (2) orthogonality ‖Qᵀ@Q − I‖ with rtol = 100·n·eps32 (residuals in FP64, tolerance FP32-level). Output factors MUST be FP32 and satisfy real QR invariants. Low precision (TF32/BF16/FP16) is allowed ONLY as an internal compute strategy if final FP32 accuracy still passes. Inputs include ill-conditioned, rank-deficient, near-rank-deficient, clustered-singular-value, near-collinear, and banded matrices, so the method must be numerically robust (naive CholeskyQR that squares the condition number will FAIL).

SCORED SHAPES (geomean of runtime, lower µs wins): batch=20,n=32; batch=40,n=176; batch=40,n=352; batch=640,n=512 (appears 4× — dominant); batch=60,n=1024 (appears 3×); batch=8,n=2048; batch=2,n=4096. The dominant workload by far is batch=640, n=512. The frontier #1 solution achieves ~422 µs geomean; a serial-cuSOLVER-loop baseline is ~131,000 µs, so genuinely batched parallelism is the entire game.

result.summary: A hand-written batched Householder QR on B200 should use the blocked compact-WY (UT) algorithm, which natively emits exactly the (H, tau) packed form torch.geqrf returns: on exit the on/above-diagonal entries of A hold R and the sub-diagonal entries hold the reflector vectors V (implicit unit diagonal), with tau the per-reflector scalars — and the product of k reflectors aggregates as I − U T⁻¹ Uᴴ (equivalently I − VTVᵀ), turning the trailing update A := (I − VTVᵀ)A into level-3 GEMMs that map onto Blackwell tensor cores. The workload splits sharply by regime: for the tiny/per-warp shapes (n=32, and within-tile work) a one-threadblock-per-matrix unblocked kernel is right, and uniquely for QR (unlike LU/Cholesky) a shared-memory or hybrid register-storage + shared-memory-communication layout beats pure warp-shuffle, because the y = vᵀC matvec costs Q·log₂(N_p2) shuffle-reduction steps versus only P steps when v and C live in shared memory. For the dominant batch=640/n=512 regime the matrix (1 MB FP32) far exceeds the ~228 KB SRAM budget, so it must be genuinely blocked (panel factorization + T-build + trailing GEMM) rather than kept resident; a persistent Triton megakernel sized to min(NUM_SMS, total_tiles) with each program looping over multiple independent matrices is the attested structural pattern for batching these, though Triton's lack of grid-level sync and register control bounds how much of a large-n factorization one cooperating program-group can own. The verified evidence is strongest on the algebra and packing (multiple primary LAPACK/FLAME sources, unanimous) and on the small-matrix design tradeoff (peer-reviewed MAGMA/ICL primary); it is thinner and partly contested on the precise SRAM/large-n cooperative-grid bounds and on FP32-accuracy-via-tensor-core (3xTF32/mixed-precision refinement) claims, which did not survive verification and remain open.

findings.claim: The blocked compact-WY/UT algorithm aggregates k Householder reflectors as H_0 H_1 ... H_{k-1} = I − U T⁻¹ Uᴴ (equivalently the LAPACK compact-WY form I − VTVᵀ with T upper triangular), and this is the exact algebraic basis for expressing the trailing update as matrix-matrix products and for the packed (H,tau) layout torch.geqrf returns.
findings.evidence: The FLAME/LAFF source (van de Geijn, UT Austin) states verbatim 'If H_0,...,H_{k-1} are Householder transformations, then H_0 H_1 ... H_{k-1} = I − U T⁻¹ Uᴴ', defining U as the Householder vectors (unit diagonal) and T as upper triangular. This is the foundational Schreiber & Van Loan (1989) compact-WY representation (Q = I + YTYᵀ, T upper triangular) that still underpins LAPACK GEQRF; the FLAME UT form and LAPACK I−VTVᵀ differ only in whether T's diagonal stores 1/tau-scaled values or tau directly. torch.geqrf wraps LAPACK GEQRF, which 'uses a compact WY transform,' stores reflector vectors below the diagonal (=V/U) with tau separate. The trailing update A:=(I−VTVᵀ)A is the level-3 GEMM form (DLARFT builds T, DLARFB applies it).
findings.confidence_note: Two primary sources (FLAME/LAFF + the 1989 SIAM compact-WY paper), unanimous verification, timeless classical NLA result.

findings.claim: The recursive panel factorization natively produces the torch.geqrf packed form: on exit the elements on and above the diagonal of A hold the n×n upper-triangular R, and the elements below the diagonal hold the reflector vectors V with the unit diagonal not stored — exactly the (H) packing the problem contract requires (square inputs, m=n).
findings.evidence: netlib geqrt3 states verbatim 'the elements on and above the diagonal contain the N-by-N upper triangular matrix R; the elements below the diagonal are the columns of V,' with Further Details adding 'The 1's along the diagonal of V are not stored in A.' This matches LAPACK DGEQRF man pages and the PyTorch torch.geqrf docs ('elements of R are stored on and above the diagonal. Elementary reflectors ... stored below the diagonal'), which feed torch.linalg.householder_product — exactly the checker's Q reconstruction. The contract's inputs are square (batch×n×n), so geqrt3's 'N-by-N upper triangular R' is precisely the contract case; the trapezoidal caveat for m≠n is irrelevant. Note: geqrt3 itself returns the compact-WY T factor, not per-reflector tau scalars, so a kernel must also emit tau separately to match geqrf's (H,tau) output.
findings.confidence_note: Primary LAPACK reference, independently corroborated by PyTorch docs; decades-stable storage convention.

findings.claim: The composite T factor for two stacked sub-panels is T = [[T1, T3],[0, T2]] with the off-diagonal coupling block T3 = −T1·(Y1ᴴ·Y2)·T2. This is the exact GEMM-friendly recurrence for assembling the T matrix recursively from two sub-panels (the level-3 alternative to LAPACK DLARFT's level-2 bordering).
findings.evidence: The canonical LAPACK reference implementation dgeqrt3.f (Elmroth-Gustavson recursive QR) contains verbatim at line 223 'Compute T3 = T(1:N1,J1:N) = -T1 Y1^H Y2 T2' and at lines 243-244 the block structure 'T = [T1 T3] / [ 0 T2]', with T1/Y1 from the first panel (line 186 'Q1 = I - Y1 T1 Y1^H') and T2/Y2 from the second (line 218 'Q2 = I - Y2 T2 Y2^H'). Independently corroborated by peer-reviewed arXiv:2409.13374 (Eq. 5.19) giving the identical T_new = [[T1, -T1*(Y1^H*Y2)*T2],[0,T2]]. In implementation the −T1(Y1ᴴY2)T2 product is evaluated via a TRMM (unit-lower-triangular top block) + GEMM (rectangular bottom block) split plus TRMM by T1/T2 — a Level-3 construction of T.
findings.confidence_note: Primary LAPACK reference implementation plus peer-reviewed corroboration, unanimous.

findings.claim: For the tiny/per-warp regime (n=32 and within-tile work), QR uniquely favors shared-memory (or a hybrid: registers for storage + shared memory for communication) over a pure register/warp-shuffle implementation — the OPPOSITE of LU and Cholesky — because the inner y = vᵀC matvec in the Householder update needs Q·log₂(N_p2) shuffle-reduction steps (N rounded up to a power of two) versus only P steps with shared memory, where each y element maps to one thread.
findings.evidence: Abdelfattah, Haidar, Tomov, Dongarra (J. Comp. Sci. 26, 2018, the definitive MAGMA/ICL work) states verbatim 'Unlike the Cholesky and LU factorizations, we observe that the shared memory version is faster than the register version, which is the opposite of our initial expectations'; that the update computes 'y = vT C, where C = A[i:N, i+1:N]'; that with shuffles 'the total number of reduction steps is Q×log2(Np2), and not Q×log2(P)'; and 'If both v and C are in shared memory, we can assign each element of y to a single thread... using Q threads, it would take only P steps to find the entire vector y.' Fig.8 shows the hybrid (register storage + shared-memory communication) beats pure shared memory. CAVEAT: this is established only for the tiny/sub-warp regime (matrices size ≤32, one warp per matrix, Pascal/Volta) — it directly informs the contract's n=32 / small per-warp shapes but does NOT transfer to the n=512 blocked regime, where the matrix fits in neither registers nor a single warp.
findings.confidence_note: Peer-reviewed primary source from the authoritative group; mechanism is reduction-arithmetic (architecture-independent), but scope is the tiny-matrix regime only.

findings.claim: A persistent Triton kernel sizes its grid to min(NUM_SMS, total_tiles) — launching at most NUM_SMS programs, each looping over multiple work units — and this structural pattern generalizes from single-matmul tiles to independent problems, making it the attested basis for a persistent one-program-per-matrix batched QR megakernel in the small-n large-batch regime.
findings.evidence: The Triton persistent-matmul tutorial gives verbatim 'grid = lambda META: (min(NUM_SMS, triton.cdiv(M, META["BLOCK_SIZE_M"]) * triton.cdiv(N, META["BLOCK_SIZE_N"])), )' with NUM_SMS = device multi_processor_count, each program looping via 'for tile_id in tl.range(start_pid, num_tiles, NUM_SMS, flatten=True)'. The PyTorch Engineering grouped-GEMM blog applies the IDENTICAL structure (grid=(NUM_SMS,1,1), same tl.range loop) to INDEPENDENT MoE experts, proving the pattern generalizes from single-matmul tiles to independent work units (the batched-QR case). Colfax frames it generally as 'grid fixed to number of SMs ... each CTA persists, processing multiple work units.' QUALIFIER: the claim is correctly hedged as the structural pattern, NOT a solved QR kernel — it does not address QR's sequential panel dependency. Also, for batch ≤ a few thousand one could alternatively launch `batch` programs directly without the min(NUM_SMS,...) cap.
findings.confidence_note: Mechanical core verbatim-confirmed (primary Triton docs); the generalization to QR is corroborated by an independent primary source but the vote was split (2-1) and the pattern alone does not solve QR's cross-program sequential dependency.

result.caveats:
SCOPE-MATCHED, NOT END-TO-END. The verified claims rigorously establish (a) the compact-WY algebra and the native (H,tau)/R-V packing, (b) the recursive T-assembly recurrence, (c) the shared-memory-vs-shuffle design tradeoff for tiny matrices, and (d) the persistent-Triton grid structure. They do NOT, on their own, constitute a complete recipe for the dominant batch=640/n=512 workload or the FP32-accuracy requirement.

WEAK / CONTESTED AREAS. Several claims central to sub-questions 3, 5, and the large-n part of 4 did NOT survive verification (vote 0-0, 1-0, or were refuted): the explicit three-GEMM trailing-update decomposition (W:=UᴴB, W:=T⁻¹W, B:=B−UW), the T = upper-triangular(UᴴU) diagonal-fixup recipe, the six-Level-3-BLAS DLARFB sequence, and — most importantly for this problem — the SRAM-budget/large-n cooperative-grid bound (the claim that a 512×512 FP32 matrix at 1 MB exceeds 228 KB SRAM and forces a blocked approach was voted 1-2, i.e., net refuted on its specific framing even though the underlying arithmetic is sound). Treat the large-n cooperative-grid necessity as plausible-but-unverified here rather than established.

NO VERIFIED EVIDENCE ON CUTE DSL OR FP32-VIA-TENSOR-CORE. Sub-question 3 (CUTLASS CuTe DSL on sm_100, tcgen05 5th-gen tensor cores) and sub-question 5 (3xTF32 / split-float FP32 emulation, mixed-precision QR with refinement surviving rtol=20·n·eps32 on ill-conditioned/rank-deficient inputs) produced NO claims that reached the confirmed set. There is therefore no verified guidance on whether TF32/BF16 internal compute can hold FP32 accuracy through the checker on the hard inputs — this is the single biggest correctness risk and is entirely unaddressed by the surviving evidence.

TRIANGLE-SOLVE PRECISION (tau): note that geqrt3-style recursive panels return the compact-WY T factor, not per-reflector tau; matching geqrf exactly requires separately producing tau (the diagonal of the elementary reflectors), which the confirmed claims flag but do not give a kernel-level recipe for.

TIME-SENSITIVITY. The LAPACK/FLAME/Schreiber-Van Loan algebra is timeless. The Triton persistent-kernel APIs (tl.range flatten=True, grid lambda) are 2024-2025 and version-sensitive; verify against the installed Triton on PyTorch 2.11. The MAGMA tiny-matrix finding is on Pascal/Volta and explicitly does not transfer to n=512 on Blackwell.
openQuestions: Can TF32 / 3xTF32 / split-float FP32 emulation on B200 tcgen05 tensor cores keep the final FP32 (H,tau) within rtol=20·n·eps32 (factor) and 100·n·eps32 (orthogonality) on the ill-conditioned, rank-deficient, near-collinear, and banded inputs — or is a true-FP32 compute path (with optional one-step iterative refinement) required for the hard cases? No surviving claim addresses this, and it is the dominant correctness risk.

What is the concrete, verified mapping of the trailing update (I−VTVᵀ)A onto tensor-core GEMMs for the n=512 regime — the three-GEMM (UᴴB → T⁻¹W → B−UW) and six-Level-3-BLAS DLARFB decompositions were proposed but did not survive verification; which exact kernel sequence and block/panel sizes are optimal for batch=640/n=512 on sm_100?

Is a single persistent megakernel actually superior to a sequence of batched-GEMM (e.g. cuBLAS/CUTLASS batched) calls for batch=640/n=512, and where is the crossover in n/batch? The persistent-grid structure is attested but its advantage over batched-GEMM dispatch for QR specifically is unverified.

Does CUTLASS CuTe DSL (Python) provide factorization examples or the fusion (panel + trailing-update) primitives needed on Blackwell, and how does one express QR's sequential down-panel dependency given Triton's lack of grid-level sync and register control? No confirmed evidence exists on CuTe DSL for this task.

refuted.claim: The block triangular factor T is computed as the upper-triangular part of U^H U, with the diagonal then divided by two OR set to the tau coefficients tau_0,...,tau_{k-1}. This gives a concrete, GEMM-friendly recipe (a single U^H U product plus a diagonal fix-up) to build T from the panel's Householder vectors and tau values — directly relevant to forming the T matrix on tensor cores.

Applying the accumulated transform to the trailing block factors into three matrix-matrix operations: W := U^H B (GEMM), W := T^{-1} W (triangular solve), then B := B - U W (GEMM), via the identity (I - U T^{-1} U^H) B = B - U(T^{-1}(U^H B)). This is precisely how the trailing update maps onto tensor-core GEMMs.

The blocked QR algorithm's trailing update for a column panel is W_12 = T_11^{-H}(U_11^H A_12 + U_21^H A_22), followed by A_12 := A_12 - U_11 W_12 and A_22 := A_22 - U_21 W_12 — giving the exact panel-trailing recurrence (factor panel via unblocked QR, FormT, then GEMM update) for a blocked implementation.

The compact-WY block reflector H (the operator applied in the trailing update of blocked QR) is expressed as H = I - V*T*V**T when reflector vectors are stored columnwise (STOREV='C'), where T is the triangular factor formed by DLARFT. This is exactly the (I - VTV**T) trailing-update operator the research question asks to map onto tensor-core GEMMs.

The order-n block reflector H is the product of k individual elementary Householder reflectors, and the multiplication order plus T's triangularity depend on DIRECT: forward gives H = H(1)H(2)...H(k) with T upper triangular, backward gives H = H(k)...H(2)H(1) with T lower triangular. This defines the panel-of-k-columns recurrence that natively produces the packed (H,tau) form geqrf returns.

tau is the per-reflector scalar coefficient: TAU(i) holds the scalar factor of elementary reflector H(i). This is the same tau vector torch.geqrf returns (one coefficient per reflector / column), establishing that the blocked algorithm's inputs map directly onto the exact problem contract's tau output.

The compact-WY block reflector that aggregates a panel of Householder reflectors is given exactly by H = I - V*T*V^T, where V holds the reflector vectors in unit-lower-triangular form and T is an N-by-N upper triangular matrix; this is the trailing-update operator the research question needs to map to tensor-core GEMMs.

The storage-efficient compact-WY representation factors Q = Q1Q2...Qk = I − YTY^T, where Y is m×k lower trapezoidal holding the k Householder vectors (each with an implicit leading 1, scaled by tau_i) and T is a k×k upper triangular matrix; this is exactly the packed (H, tau) form torch.geqrf returns, so the blocked algorithm natively produces it. For k=2, T = [[tau1, −tau1·u1^T·u2·tau2],[0, tau2]].

The T matrix for a split k = k1 + k2 is built by the block formula T = [[T1, −T1·(Y1^T·Y2)·T2],[0, T2]], where T1, T2 are the triangular factors of the two sub-blocks and Y=(Y1,Y2) is concatenation. This off-diagonal coupling block −T1(Y1^T Y2)T2 is computed entirely by GEMM (Y1^T·Y2) and two TRMM operations, giving a Level-3 (matrix–matrix) construction of T instead of LAPACK DLARFT's Level-2 bordering.

The trailing-matrix update applying Q^T = I − Y·T^T·Y^T to a block C (i.e. Ĉ = Q^T C = C − Y·T^T·(Y^T·C)) is implemented as a fixed sequence of six Level-3 BLAS calls — two TRMM (with the unit-triangular top block Y1), two GEMM (with the rectangular bottom block Y2), one TRMM by T^T, and a matrix subtract — for a total of kn(4m−k−1) FLOPs; partitioning Y=[Y1;Y2] with Y1 k×k unit lower triangular and Y2 (m−k)×k. This is the routine the paper calls DQTC (equivalent to LAPACK DLARFB).

A product of r Householder matrices Q = P_1...P_r (each m x m) can be written in the compact-WY form Q = I + Y*T*Y^T, where Y is m x r and T is r x r upper triangular. This is the exact representation that blocked Householder QR (and the geqrf packed H/tau form) accumulates, and the single dense Y*T*Y^T product is what maps the trailing update A := (I - V*T*V^T)*A onto a tensor-core GEMM.

The entire motivation for the WY / compact-WY representation is to recast the QR update from matrix-vector (level-2 BLAS) operations into matrix-matrix (level-3 BLAS) operations, which is precisely the transformation needed to feed the trailing-update as a tensor-core GEMM on Blackwell.

Tile QR decomposes the factorization into four computational kernels (LAPACK-style names SGEQRT, STSQRT, SLARFB, SSSRFB) that operate on small square tiles; SGEQRT factors a diagonal tile producing R, a unit-lower-triangular V of Householder reflectors, AND the compact-WY upper-triangular T matrix (stored separately), so the algorithm natively produces the V/tau-style reflector representation rather than an explicit Q. This maps directly onto the research question's per-tile panel + trailing-GEMM structure.

The compact-WY representation lets the trailing update be expressed as level-3 BLAS (GEMM): it requires one T matrix of size equal to the panel width per panel, and the overhead of manipulating T is negligible because T is much smaller than the panel height. This is exactly the (I − VTVᵀ)A → tensor-core GEMM mapping the research question asks about, with its cost amortization condition.

There is a quantified extra-flops vs memory-intensity tradeoff: naive per-tile T construction (one T per square tile) costs ~25% more operations than standard QR, while a pure level-2-BLAS update has the same flop count as standard QR (2MN² − 2/3 N³) but performs poorly because it is memory-bound. The performance sweet spot is inner-blocking inside the tile, with T stored as triangular blocks of the inner block size on the diagonal. This directly informs block-size choice for the trailing-update GEMM strategy.

For batched factorization of tiny matrices (size up to 32), the optimal design is one-kernel/one-CUDA-threadblock-per-matrix with fully unblocked computation and read/write-each-matrix-exactly-once, because the computation is memory-bound at these sizes and the entire matrix stays cached in fast memory (registers or shared memory) for the whole factorization, making LAPACK-style panel blocking pointless.

A 1D thread configuration (N threads per matrix) decisively outperforms a 2D (N×N threads) configuration for batched tiny-matrix factorization, because the 2D layout (e.g. 256 threads for a 16×16 matrix) caps resident threadblocks per SM and kills occupancy; measured speedups are 10.5×/9.6× (single/double) for Cholesky and ~9× or more for LU and QR on a Pascal P100.

Triton (unlike CUDA) provides no programmer access to GPU registers, so a kernel cannot implement a custom register-caching strategy and must instead rely on Triton's compiler to manage shared-memory/register placement. This is a concrete expressibility limit for hand-written QR panel kernels that want reflector vectors / T-matrix tiles pinned in registers.

Triton has no grid-level synchronization between programs and cannot communicate values between programs via HBM; in the one-program-per-matrix (per-head) design this caps the per-program working dimension (head dimension limited to 128 forward / 64 backward on H100). A single-threadblock unblocked Householder QR in Triton is therefore size-bounded by what fits without cross-program sync, and large n (e.g. 512/1024) cannot be handled by one cooperating program-group in Triton the way a CUDA cooperative grid can.

On an H100/Hopper-class SM the register file is 256 KB and shared memory is up to 228 KB per SM/block; a 768x768 weight matrix (~4 MB) therefore cannot fit on one SM and must be sharded across multiple SMs in a cooperative grid group that synchronizes at grid level. This directly bounds the largest n a one-matrix-per-threadblock QR can keep resident: a 512x512 FP32 panel/matrix is 1 MB, far exceeding 228 KB SRAM, so only column-panel tiles (not the full matrix) fit in shared memory, forcing a blocked/cooperative-grid approach for large n.
